tr.td: The Kharqamar checkpost near Boya, North Waziristan, in Pakistan's former tribal districts
Activists of the Pashtun Tahaffuz Movement (PTM), led on the day by its two National Assembly members, Mohsin Dawar and Ali Wazir, and soldiers of the army post
Disputed: the military first said three, a later military statement said at least eight, and a government report counted 13 local people and one soldier dead
The Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government withdrew the case on 14 October 2020, and both lawmakers were acquitted of all charges
The army's media wing said a group led by Dawar and Wazir "assaulted" the post, and that five soldiers were injured in the firing
The movement said the procession was unarmed and that soldiers fired on protesters; Dawar said the shooting began after the crowd cheered
A two-page Special Situation Report dated 28 May, submitted by the North Waziristan deputy commissioner, counted 13 local dead, 25 wounded, one soldier dead and seven soldiers hurt
Wazir was taken into custody at the site with eight others; Dawar surrendered on 30 May after a jirga intervened
A curfew in North Waziristan, with mobile, landline and internet services cut
An FIR at the Counter-Terrorism Department police station in Bannu, under the Pakistan Penal Code, the Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance and Section 7 of the Anti-Terrorism Act
Amnesty International and the Human Rights Commission of Pakistan asked for independent investigations; the pages reviewed report no completed independent inquiry
The government announced payments to the families of those killed, and the provincial government later distributed cheques

content.p: On the morning of Sunday 26 May 2019, gunfire broke out at a military checkpost in the Kharqamar area of North Waziristan, a district on the Afghan border where the army had run a security operation since 2014. The army said a group led by two members of parliament from the Pashtun Tahaffuz Movement attacked the post. The movement said its unarmed supporters were shot by soldiers. The official toll and the movement's toll did not match in the reports reviewed.
content.h2: Background: a movement and a warning
content.p: The Pashtun Tahaffuz Movement grew out of protests in early 2018 over the killing of Naqeebullah Mehsud, a young man from South Waziristan who was picked up in Karachi by a senior police officer and killed, after being labelled a terrorist. The protests became a campaign against extrajudicial killings, enforced disappearances and the landmines left in the tribal districts. Al Jazeera described its three main demands as the clearance of unexploded ordnance, an end to extrajudicial killings in the war against armed groups, and accountability for enforced disappearances.

The movement's relations with the army worsened through spring 2019. In April 2019, the military's spokesman, Major General Asif Ghafoor, warned that those "playing into the hands of others" had run out of time. The army later read out a charge sheet accusing the movement of receiving money from foreign intelligence agencies, a claim the movement denied. Dawar and Wazir had been elected to the National Assembly from North Waziristan in the 2018 general election.

An internal government report, which Dawn later published, listed a run of attacks in the district in April and early May 2019 that killed several soldiers. Residents of the area had held a sit-in over what they described as abuses during a military search operation. On 25 May, after talks with a jirga, the authorities agreed to release one detained man on condition that the protest would end, according to the same report. The report says the protest resumed that night, and that the two lawmakers were expected to join it the next morning.

Dawar and Wazir set out with a group of supporters. Their accounts and the army's differ at almost every step. The army's report says the two lawmakers reached the post at about 9:30 a.m. with roughly 300 supporters, and that troops at the first barrier asked them to take another route. It says Wazir used abusive language and urged the crowd to attack the post, and that protesters began throwing stones while armed men with the lawmakers opened fire. The report says the soldiers fired warning shots first and then fired at positions across a causeway from which they were being shot at.

Dawar told Al Jazeera that the group crossed a second barrier and reached the protesters, who began cheering, and that firing started from behind them. He said he thought at first that it was aerial firing, until he saw two men beside him fall. Al Jazeera reported that at least two pieces of video shared by the movement appeared to back this account, with shots heard after the crowd crossed a barrier. Al Jazeera also said that the military's security source described the crossing of the barrier as an aggressive act, and that check posts are no-go areas.

Several cellphone videos that circulated on social media appeared to show protesters without weapons, according to VOA, which said it could not verify any of them independently. Reporters could not reach the area. Mobile and internet services were cut, and a curfew was imposed on North Waziristan.

The early figures were low and rose over the following days. The army's first statement, issued in the afternoon, said three people were killed and 15 wounded, including five soldiers. On the next day a military statement put the death toll at at least eight, after five more bodies were found in the area. The military's figure was given in its statement to Al Jazeera, which could not verify it independently.

The government report, submitted on 28 May and published by Dawn on 31 May, gave a much higher count. It listed 13 local people dead and 25 wounded, and one soldier dead with seven soldiers hurt. The report said that two bodies were found within 40 to 50 metres of the post, six more 150 to 400 metres away, and five more about 1,500 metres off.

The movement's figures were higher still. A Himal Southasian interview published in June 2019 quoted early reports of 13 dead, then unverified claims of more than 20, and described the event as the "Khar Qamar massacre". Himal said these numbers could not be verified. Amnesty International, on 27 May, had spoken of at least three activists killed. Each figure should be read with the name of the party that gave it.

The army said Wazir was arrested with eight others, and that Dawar was at large after inciting the crowd. Wazir was held at the site, according to Dawn's later reporting. Dawar told Al Jazeera on 28 May that he was in hiding and feared for his life. He later gave himself up to the administration on 30 May, once a jirga had stepped in, and officials announced payments to the families of those killed and hurt, Dawn reported.

Both lawmakers were charged under the Anti-Terrorism Act and the Pakistan Penal Code, the Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance also cited. Dawn reported that the FIR, filed at the Counter-Terrorism Department police station in Bannu, alleged that the two men and seven other PTM leaders carried firearms, and that 300 to 350 supporters carried sticks. The complaint said the lawmakers had approached the post and started firing. The defence lawyers argued that the petitioners were unarmed and that videos showed this.

In August 2019, the anti-terrorism court in Bannu rejected the bail petitions in the Kharqamar case. In a separate case over a roadside bomb in Doga Macha, which killed four army officers and for which an FIR was registered on 7 June, the same court accepted the two men's bail pleas, with sureties of Rs80,000 each, Dawn reported.

Amnesty International called on the government to "immediately order an independent and effective investigation" into the deaths, and warned that if soldiers had used live ammunition unlawfully, it would be a serious violation of international law. The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan expressed alarm and said the events could create a lasting split between the tribal districts and the state. The Pakistan Bar Council voiced great concern. Opposition parties demanded a probe; the ruling Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf backed the army's version, according to VOA.

Several politicians urged the government to negotiate with the movement rather than use force. Bilawal Bhutto Zardari, the chairperson of the PPP, asked how a lawmaker could lead an attack on a checkpost, and said the facts would be established. The movement itself said it would keep its protest peaceful.

In March 2020 the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa government filed an application at the Bannu anti-terrorism court saying it wished to withdraw the prosecution, citing the prevailing situation. The case was transferred to an anti-terrorism court in Abbottabad. Geo reported that the move followed the movement's acceptance of a government offer of talks, and that the movement had urged the government to take "confidence-building measures".

On 14 October 2020 the case was withdrawn, and Dawar and Wazir were acquitted of all charges, Geo and Pakistan Today reported. Pakistan Today said the provincial government had distributed compensation cheques to the families of the victims.

Who fired first is still contested. The army's account says the lawmakers' group attacked the post; the movement says the protesters were shot without provocation. No independent investigation of the shooting appears in the pages reviewed, and no independent corroboration was found for either account, Dawn noted at the time. The death toll also remains in dispute: the military's early figures of three and eight, the government report's 13 local people and one soldier, and the higher figures claimed by the movement cannot all be reconciled. The soldiers' injuries are reported as five by the army and as seven by the government report. A separate local protest, against the detention of two men, was described by a military security source as having nothing to do with the movement. Dawar said the people of the area had been protesting, and that he had gone to find out what had happened.
